newsitem.title: USA: Fed banks sought discount rate hike for much of 96.
newsitem.headline: Fed banks sought discount rate hike for much of 96.

text.p: The Federal Reserve board was under pressure from regional Fed banks to hike the discount rate throughout the second half of last year, but resisted, newly released minutes of decision-making sessions showed on Thursday.
The pressure began as far back as May when two banks began requesting an increase in the rate and seemed to reach a high point in September and October before ebbing late in the year.

This is the first time that the Fed has broadly disseminated the minutes from its regular weekly dicussion about the discount rate, which is the rate that the U.S. central bank charges for infrequent loans to commercial banks.
The minutes have been available before but only at special request.

In a widely quoted press leak from the closed-door sessions, Reuters reported on Sept 17 that eight of the 12 regional Fed banks had sought an increase in the 5.0-percent discount rate and that three wanted a half-point rise.
The minutes of the Fed Board's Sept 16 meeting confirm that was indeed the case.
However, it identified the three banks that wanted the half-point increase as Boston, Richmond and St. Louis, rather than Minneapolis, Richmond and San Francisco as reported by Reuters.
The Fed asked the Federal Bureau of Investigation to investigate the leak to Reuters.
According to the minutes of the Sept 16 meeting, the regional banks cited increased price pressures and the risk of rising inflation in pressing the board for a discount-rate increase at that time.
Pressure from the regional Federal Reserve banks began to ebb in November as the economy showed signs of slowing.

By the end of the year, only one regional Fed bank, from St Louis, was still requesting a discount rate increase, but only by a quarter percentage point, according to the minutes of the December 20 meeting.
The central bank this week raised its target for the federal funds rate -- the rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight money -- by a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent.
It left the discount rate steady at 5.0 percent. The discount rate has not been changed since Jan 31, 1996, when it and the federal funds rate each were cut by a quarter percentage point.
